q: A parent mentions the child started a new medication. The RBT should:
a: Document it and inform the supervisor promptly
Leave it out of the note as private medical data
Adjust the program to offset side effects
Pause sessions until the BCBA responds
e: Variables that may affect progress (illness, medication, schedule) are reported in a timely manner (E.3).

q: You notice the data look off and aren't sure how to proceed. You should:
a: Seek clinical direction from the supervisor
Use professional judgment and decide alone
Let the caregiver choose how to proceed
Pause data collection until it looks right
e: Seek and prioritize clinical direction through the chain of command (E.2).

q: RBTs relay caregiver concerns and suggestions to the supervisor in a timely manner.
e: True. Communicating team concerns to the supervisor is an RBT task (E.1).

q: Session notes must be:
a: Accurate, objective, and completed on time
Written from memory within a few days
Focused on overall impressions of the day
Required only when insurance requests them
e: Notes must objectively reflect what occurred and meet legal/regulatory/workplace rules (E.4).

q: You're asked to run a procedure you've never been trained on. You should:
a: Ask your supervisor for training first
Look it up online and proceed
Have a coworker show you quickly
e: Provide services only after demonstrating competence — get proper training first (F.2).

q: RBTs may provide services only:
e: RBTs work only under ongoing supervision from a qualifying supervisor (F.3).

q: A neighbor asks how a client you both know is doing. You:
a: Do not share any client information
e: Protect confidential information — disclose nothing, not even that they're a client (F.5).

q: A caregiver sends you a social-media friend request. Best practice is to:
a: Decline and keep the relationship professional
Accept but keep the account fully private
Ask the BCBA to accept on your behalf
e: Avoid public/social-media entanglements that blur professional boundaries (F.6).

q: Babysitting your client for pay on weekends is an example of a:
e: A multiple relationship creates conflict-of-interest risk and should be avoided (F.7).

q: A family offers you an expensive gift. Following the ethics code, you:
a: Decline, following the BACB gift guidelines
Accept it warmly to respect the gesture
Accept it but leave it out of the record
Exchange it for additional session time
e: Adhere to the BACB gift-giving/receiving guidelines; significant gifts are declined (F.8).

q: Ongoing cultural humility and responsiveness means:
a: Examining your biases and respecting family values
Applying the clinic standard to every family
Treating every family exactly the same way
Leaving cultural topics to the caregivers
e: Cultural humility means identifying personal biases and responding respectfully to each family (F.10).

q: Maintaining client dignity includes:
a: Sharing session stories with other families
e: Core ethics: treat others with compassion, dignity, and respect (F.1).

q: Accepting and acting on supervisor feedback is an expected professional skill for RBTs.
e: True. Accepting feedback and collaborating are required interpersonal/professional skills (F.9).

q: Three of these are part of cultural responsiveness. Which does NOT belong?
a: Use the same materials and style with every family
e: A one-size-fits-all approach is the opposite of cultural responsiveness (F.10) — the other three actively adapt to the family.

q: Negative reinforcement:
a: Removes a stimulus to INCREASE a behavior
Adds a stimulus to increase a behavior
Removes a stimulus to decrease a behavior
Adds a stimulus to decrease a behavior
e: Negative = remove; reinforcement = behavior increases. Something aversive is taken away.

q: A child does chores and the nagging stops; chores then increase. This is:
e: Removing the nagging (aversive) makes chores more likely — negative reinforcement (escape).

q: A spray of water is added and nail-biting decreases. This is:
e: Adding a stimulus that decreases behavior is positive punishment.

q: Tokens are removed after a behavior and the behavior decreases. This is:
e: Removing a reinforcer to decrease behavior is negative punishment — here, response cost.

q: The defining feature of a reinforcer is that it:
a: It increases the future frequency of behavior
It feels pleasant to the person receiving it
It is an item the person strongly prefers
It is delivered immediately after behavior
e: Reinforcement is defined by its effect — the behavior increases — not by how it feels.

q: Reinforcement always increases behavior and punishment always decreases it, whether positive or negative.
e: True. “Positive/negative” = add/remove; “reinforcement/punishment” = increase/decrease.

q: Three of these increase behavior. Which is the odd one out?
e: Response cost is punishment — it decreases behavior. The others strengthen it.

q: A child says “cookie” because they want a cookie (motivated by deprivation). This is a:
e: A mand is a request under motivation (an MO); it specifies its own reinforcer.

q: A child sees a dog and says “dog” with no specific reward wanted. This is a:
e: A tact labels something in the environment; it's evoked by contact with the item.

q: You say “ball” and the child repeats “ball.” This is an:
e: An echoic is a vocal copy with point-to-point correspondence to what was heard.

q: You ask “What do you ride?” and the child says “bike” — no bike present. This is an:
e: An intraverbal answers verbal stimuli without point-to-point correspondence (conversation, fill-ins).

q: Reading the written word “cat” aloud is a:
e: Textual behavior is reading written words aloud; transcription is writing/spelling what's heard.

q: The verbal operant usually taught first, because it's tied to motivation and benefits the learner directly, is the:
e: Mands are taught first — requesting gets the learner what they want and builds communication.

q: Three of these are verbal operants. Which is the odd one out?
e: A prompt is a teaching aid, not a verbal operant. Mand, tact, and intraverbal are operants.

q: Going without water for hours makes water more valuable and increases water-seeking. This is a(n):
e: An EO increases the value of a reinforcer and the behavior that gets it (deprivation).

q: Just after a big meal, food is less valuable and food-seeking drops. This is a(n):
e: An AO decreases a reinforcer's value and the behavior it evokes (satiation).

q: During a community outing, a client who has been walking for 30 minutes without a break becomes highly motivated by a rest on a bench. The RBT recognizes that fatigue temporarily changed the ___ of rest as a reinforcer.
e: Fatigue is an establishing operation that increases the value of rest. Topography describes behavior form; latency and IOA are measurement concepts, not MO effects.

q: A motivating operation is an antecedent that changes how much a consequence is currently wanted.
e: True. An MO alters the momentary value of a reinforcer and the behavior that produces it.

q: A pop quiz that could happen any class period reinforces studying on a ___ schedule.
e: Reinforcement tied to unpredictable time = variable interval.

q: A paycheck delivered every two weeks is a ___ schedule.
e: A set, predictable time period = fixed interval. This is not Variable interval because it does not match the scenario.

q: A client reliably mands for break with FR-1 reinforcement. The BCBA directs the RBT to require 2 mands per break, then 5, then 10 across weeks. This progression is called:
e: Increasing the response requirement (FR-2 → FR-5 → FR-10) is schedule thinning. Shaping changes response topography; chaining sequences steps; fading reduces prompts.

q: Reinforcing hand-raising instead of shouting out is:
e: DRA reinforces a specific alternative behavior in place of the problem behavior.

q: Reinforcing sitting — which physically cannot co-occur with running — is:
e: DRI reinforces a behavior that is physically incompatible with the target.

q: Reinforcing fewer occurrences (e.g., 3 or fewer requests per session) is:
e: DRL reinforces reduced rates of a behavior that's acceptable in moderation.

q: A-B-C recording captures antecedent, behavior, and:
e: A-B-C = Antecedent, Behavior, Consequence — a descriptive assessment tool.

q: Which is the LEAST direct way to identify a behavior's function?
a: An indirect interview or rating scale
e: Indirect methods rely on others' reports rather than observing behavior directly.

q: Which task is OUTSIDE the RBT scope of practice?
a: Creating or modifying the treatment plan
e: Designing or changing the plan is the BCBA's job. RBTs implement and report.

q: If a client withdraws assent (shows they don't want to continue), the RBT should note it and respond appropriately rather than force the task.
e: True. Respecting assent withdrawal protects the client and is part of ethical, dignified practice.

q: Which phrase belongs in an objective session note?
a: Engaged in 12 minutes of independent play
Was in a great mood all session
e: Objective notes record observable, measurable events — not moods or interpretations (E.4).

q: When should a session note be written?
a: During or immediately after the session
A few days later from memory
At the end of the month
e: Notes are completed contemporaneously so they're accurate and complete (E.4).

q: Which statement is NOT appropriate for a session note?
a: Client eloped from the table twice
e: “Manipulative” is an interpretation, not an observation. Notes stay objective (E.4).

q: Session notes should record what was observed, not the RBT's opinions or interpretations.
e: True. Documentation must be objective and factual (E.4).

q: A client seems unusually drowsy after a recent medication change. The RBT should:
a: Document it and notify the supervisor
Adjust the program to be easier
e: Report variables that may affect the client or the data in a timely manner (E.3).

q: The family mentions the client didn't sleep and skipped breakfast. The RBT should:
a: Note it — setting events can affect data — and tell the supervisor
Leave it out; sleep is not behavioral data
Cancel the session until routines resume
Rewrite the goals around the missed meal
e: Sleep, illness, and meals are variables that can affect behavior — document and report them (E.3).

q: When unsure how to run part of a program, the RBT should:
a: Ask the supervising BCBA for direction
Have the caregiver demonstrate it first
Set that program aside for the session
e: Seek and prioritize clinical direction through the chain of command (E.2).

q: A parent asks the RBT to add a brand-new goal to the session. The RBT should:
a: Refer the request to the supervisor
e: Adding or changing goals is the BCBA's role; relay the request up the chain (E.1/E.2).

q: The RBT feels a program no longer seems to be working. The best action is to:
a: Communicate the concern to the supervisor promptly
Quietly stop running it until asked
Give it a few more months unchanged
e: Relay team concerns and suggestions to the supervisor in a timely manner (E.1).

q: RBTs should relay caregiver clinical questions to the supervisor rather than answering them independently.
e: True. Clinical questions go up the chain of command; the RBT communicates them to the supervisor (E.1/E.2).

q: Three of these should be reported to the supervisor promptly. Which does NOT belong?
e: A favorite color isn't an urgent report. Medications, injuries, and schedule changes can affect care and data (E.3).

q: Accurate documentation matters because notes may be used for:
a: The RBT's personal record of the day
e: Notes must meet legal, regulatory, and workplace requirements — they carry real weight (E.4).

q: During snack time, a client cries and the RBT immediately provides a preferred cracker. Crying increases the next day. The most likely function is:
e: The crying is followed by access to a tangible (cracker). Attention would require social reaction; escape would remove a demand; automatic would occur without anyone present.

q: A student tells jokes during instruction and peers turn toward the student and laugh. Joking increases. The most likely function is:
e: Attention from peers maintains the behavior. No tangible is gained and no demand is removed.

q: When a difficult math sheet is presented, a learner pushes the materials away and is sent to the break area, ending the task. Pushing materials away increases. Function?
e: Escape/avoidance — the behavior removes or postpones the non-preferred task.

q: A client hand-flaps in an empty room with no demands and no one attending. The behavior persists unchanged. The most likely function is:
e: Automatic reinforcement — sensory consequences maintain the behavior without social mediation.

q: A BCBA asks the RBT to identify why a behavior keeps occurring. The RBT should report the behavior's:
e: Function = the environmental reason the behavior is reinforced. Topography is form; latency and IOA are measurement concepts.

q: A client grabs a peer's tablet and begins playing. Grabbing increases across sessions. Most likely function?
e: The client gains access to a tangible (the tablet).

q: After a client completes a worksheet, the RBT delivers praise and a preferred sticker. The client begins completing more worksheets. This consequence is an example of:
e: Positive reinforcement: a stimulus (praise/sticker) is added after the behavior and the behavior increases. Negative reinforcement would remove an aversive; punishment would decrease behavior.

q: A client screams during toothbrushing. When the RBT stops brushing, screaming increases the next day. Removing brushing is functioning as:
e: Negative reinforcement: an aversive event (brushing) is removed when screaming occurs, and screaming increases. This is escape-maintained behavior, not punishment.

q: A teacher adds extra homework after a student throws materials, and throwing decreases. This is:
e: Positive punishment: an aversive stimulus (extra homework) is added and the behavior decreases. Removing a preferred item would be negative punishment.

q: Tokens are removed after a client hits, and hitting decreases. This is best described as:
e: Negative punishment: a preferred stimulus (tokens) is removed and hitting decreases. Response cost is a common form used in token economies.

q: An RBT delivers praise and a token each time a client uses a communication card instead of screaming. Screaming is placed on extinction. This package is best described as:
e: DRA reinforces an appropriate alternative (communication card) while withholding reinforcement for screaming (extinction of the problem behavior).

q: Reinforcement is delivered for hands-in-lap while reinforcement for hitting is withheld. Hitting and hands-in-lap cannot occur at the same time. This is:
e: DRI — the replacement behavior is incompatible with the problem behavior. DRA does not require incompatibility.

q: An RBT delivers a reinforcer if no aggression occurs for a 2-minute interval. Which procedure is this?
e: DRO (differential reinforcement of other behavior) reinforces intervals with zero occurrences of the target behavior.

q: An RBT is recording data on how often a client engages in aggression. The client engaged in 15 occurrences of aggression during the 90-minute session. What should the RBT record as the response rate per hour for aggression in that session?
e: Rate standardizes count by time. 15 ÷ 1.5 hours = 10 per hour. Always match the unit in the question (here, per hour).

q: While out to dinner, an RBT's friend asks whether a child at their church is the RBT's client and uses ABA services. What is the BEST response?
a: Confirm the child is a client but decline to share treatment details
Tell the friend you work with the child and ask them not to tell anyone
Say you cannot discuss the child but you can share information about the family
Decline to confirm or deny whether the person is a client, citing confidentiality
e: Best practice: do not confirm or deny client status (HIPAA/confidentiality). Option A still confirms client status; D protects privacy without disclosure.

q: An RBT is instructed to deliver a reinforcer every time a student raises their hand and to ignore shouting out. Which differential reinforcement procedure is being implemented?
e: DRA reinforces an appropriate alternative behavior (hand-raising) while withholding reinforcement for the problem behavior (shouting). DRO would reinforce intervals with no shouting, regardless of what else occurs.

q: Which session note entry is objective and appropriate for the permanent record?
a: Client completed 8 of 10 tact trials with 2 gestural prompts
Client had a wonderful attitude today
e: Objective notes describe observable, measurable events. Attitude, intent, and motivation labels are subjective interpretations.

q: A caregiver reports the client started a new medication yesterday. The RBT should:
a: Document the report and notify the supervising BCBA promptly
Wait until the next team meeting to mention it
Skip programming until medication is stable
e: Medication changes may affect behavior and data. RBTs document and report promptly (E.3) but do not change programs without supervision.

q: The RBT is unsure how to implement a revised prompt-fading step in the behavior plan. The RBT should:
a: Contact the supervising BCBA for clinical direction
Use full physical prompts until the next session
Ask the caregiver how they want it done
Skip the program and collect only ABC data
e: RBTs seek clinical direction through the chain of command when uncertain (E.2).

q: A parent requests that the RBT add a new home goal not in the written plan. The RBT should:
a: Relay the request to the supervising BCBA
Add the goal for today only
Write a new goal and begin teaching it
e: Program changes are the BCBA's responsibility. The RBT communicates caregiver requests to the supervisor (E.1/E.2).

q: When should session notes be completed?
a: During or immediately after the session
At the end of the week from memory
After the BCBA reviews the data
e: Contemporaneous documentation supports accuracy and meets legal/workplace requirements (E.4).

q: The client arrives after a poor night of sleep and has not eaten breakfast. The RBT should:
a: Record the variables and inform the supervisor
Suspend data collection for the session
Raise demands to test motivation levels
Note it only if problem behavior occurs
e: Setting events (sleep, meals) can affect behavior and data quality. Document and report in a timely manner.

q: Which statement violates objective documentation standards?
a: The client was noncompliant and defiant
The client refused the demand 3 of 5 opportunities
The client left the table for 45 seconds
The client used the FERB on 4 of 6 opportunities
e: "Noncompliant and defiant" are subjective labels. Counts, durations, and objective descriptions belong in session notes.

q: Data collected today appear inconsistent with the behavior plan definition. The RBT should:
a: Notify the supervising BCBA and follow their direction
Change the definition to match what was recorded
Continue collecting until the pattern is clear
e: Data integrity issues require supervisor consultation — RBTs do not unilaterally alter definitions or discard data.

q: A neighbor recognizes the RBT and asks which clients they work with. The RBT should:
a: Decline to discuss any client-related information
Confirm clients but not share goals
Discuss clients if the neighbor also works in schools
e: Protect confidentiality — no client information should be disclosed in casual conversation, including confirming client status.

q: A caregiver invites the RBT to a personal social media group for "team updates." The best response is to:
a: Decline and use approved professional channels
Join but stay a silent observer
Join and share weekly progress photos
Join only alongside the supervising BCBA
e: Professional boundaries limit social-media entanglements that blur the therapeutic relationship (F.6).

q: A family offers the RBT paid babysitting on weekends. This is problematic because it creates a:
e: A multiple relationship can impair objectivity and create conflicts of interest (F.7).
